newsitem.title: USA: FAA to begin hearing into ValuJet crash.
newsitem.headline: FAA to begin hearing into ValuJet crash.

text.p: Six months after ValuJet Inc.'s Flight 592 tumbled from the Florida skies, the official cause of the disaster remains undetermined, but the crash may prove to be a milestone in U.S. aviation history.

The National Transportation Safety Board will open a weeklong hearing on Monday to further the investigation into the crash of the DC-9, which plunged into Florida's Everglades on May 11, killing all 110 people on board.
"In this day and age, accidents like this one just should not happen," NTSB board member John Goglia, who will preside over the hearing, said in a statement.

Though determination of the cause is probably still weeks or months away, much has been learned, and much has changed, since the jet sank into the muck of the Everglades, spurring what officials at the time called the longest and most arduous recovery effort in aviation history.

The crash prompted the temporary grounding of ValuJet, a high-level shake-up at the Federal Aviation Administration, a re-examination of start-up airlines and a new set of proposals for fire safety on passenger planes.

The Atlanta-bound jet had been in the air only five minutes out of Miami International Airport when fire was detected and the crew said that it had to return immediately. It crashed 13 minutes after take-off.

Almost from the start of the crash probe, investigators focused on boxes of oxygen canisters loaded in the jet's cargo hold, believing they may have started or fueled a ferocious fire that eventually spread into the passenger compartment.

Investigators suspect those canisters, used to make oxygen for passengers' masks in the event of an emergency, may have sparked a fire that crippled the plane's control cables, leaving the pilots unable to steer it.

The canisters, packed by SabreTech, one of the nation's largest aircraft maintenance contractors, were removed from MD-80 jets belonging to ValuJet and may have been improperly secured and loaded for shipping, according to the initial findings of the investigation.

The crash raised serious questions about the shipping of hazardous materials on passenger aircraft and why federal regulators had not previously required fire detection and suppression systems in cargo holds.

On Thursday, four days before the hearings, the FAA announced new safety proposals to require such equipment in cargo compartments of all commercial passenger aircraft. Under those proposals, 2,800 older aircraft in the U.S. fleet would have to be outfitted with the fire safety equipment.
The agency also said it planned to ban the transportation of oxidizing materials, such as the generators on the ValuJet plane, on commercial passenger aircraft.
The hearing may include examination of a simulation conducted this month that reportedly showed that a fire similar to the one on Flight 592 spread quickly and disabled the plane's control cables.

NTSB investigators will be called to testify along with officials of ValuJet, which was grounded for nearly three months after the accident while regulators assessed whether the airline was fit to fly. The no-frills airline began operating again in September on a severely curtailed schedule.
The hearings were likely to recall horrifying memories of the crash for the families of victims, some of whom have been campaigning for changes in air safety regulations.
Only 65 victims were identified from body parts pulled from the Everglades. Remains of unidentified victims were buried in a separate plots in a common grave at a Miami cemetery.
A special section of seats at the hearing will be set aside for family and friends of the victims, but it was uncertain how many would attend.

"It is a personal decision. But it will be a very emotional event," said Miami attorney Steven Marks, who represents 18 families of crash victims. "I have not encouraged or discouraged clients. But if I were a victim I would not want to be present."
